Course 17

Brain and behaviour

Neurons, brain regions, plasticity and what neuroscience can and cannot tell us.

Lesson 4. What neuroscience can and cannot say

1 · Lesson

Techniques such as functional magnetic resonance imaging (which measures changes in blood flow) or electroencephalography (which records electrical activity) have made it possible to study the working brain. They have contributed a great deal, but their results are often oversimplified when reported.

That an area "lights up" during a task does not mean it is "the centre" of that function, or that a person is a certain way. Most studies compare averages of small groups, and the images are the product of many statistical analyses. One famous study detected "significant" activity in the brain of a dead salmon, to show the risk of not correcting analyses properly.

Explanations with brain images are more persuasive, even when they add nothing. Neuroscience and psychology complement each other: knowing what happens in the brain does not replace understanding a person's thoughts, history and context.

2 · Example

In one experiment, people read weak explanations of psychological phenomena. When an irrelevant sentence about the brain was added, non-experts rated them as more satisfying. It is the seductive allure of neuroscience.

3 · Activity

Find a news story that says "scientists discover the brain area for…". Note how many people took part, whether it was in humans and whether the story links to the original study.
